findings.suggestion: Preserve piedod as a familiar singular apology; for a stranger-facing default consider piedodiet, with the familiar context retained in reference guidance.
findings.reason: Piedod is valid everyday Latvian addressed to one familiar person. It should not be presented as an all-context polite apology. MLVV piedot sense 2 contrasts Piedodiet, cik ir pulkstenis? with Piedod, mīļā. This is register guidance, not a finding that the existing casual form is wrong.

findings.suggestion: Keep neatliekamā palīdzība for emergency medical assistance/service; specify that ambulance here means calling the service, rather than naming the vehicle.
findings.reason: The existing phrase is useful and understandable in emergencies and the practical request vocab-0505. English ambulance can name the vehicle, while the LV expression names assistance/service; a vehicle-specific meaning would need separate wording. Source needed for this editorial scope distinction.

findings.suggestion: Remove kas (vocab-0092) as a distractor for who/кто; retain kurš only with the which-person/which-one distinction explained. Review this pair together before any later correction.
findings.reason: Actual EN→LV and RU→LV row offers kurš as correct and kas as wrong, although kas asks about an unknown person as well as a thing (MLVV examples Kas runā? and Kas ir grāmatas autors?). Kurš selects a person or thing from a set. Both can answer an unqualified who prompt; replacing kurš with kas alone would collide with vocab-0092.

findings.suggestion: Keep kas for what, but document that it also means who in person questions; do not teach kas=what and kurš=who as an exclusive one-to-one division.
findings.reason: This valid translation has a broader everyday scope than the isolated English/Russian what/что label. Its actual appearance as a wrong answer in vocab-0091 creates the high-priority ambiguity recorded there. The current vocab-0092 row itself has no kurš distractor.

findings.suggestion: Keep zīdainis and clarify baby/infant in the first year of life.
findings.reason: MLVV defines zīdainis as a child in the first year. This agrees with Russian младенец; broad English baby should not imply that the LV word applies equally to toddlers. Existing form is standard, not an unnecessarily rare variant.

findings.suggestion: Keep skolēns; clarify school pupil/school student in the shared meaning and English learner gloss.
findings.reason: MLVV defines skolēns as a school pupil. Russian школьник supports this sense. Generic English student can include university students, which would ordinarily call for students in Latvian. The LV form is suitable for this school-age course; its intended school sense needs to remain explicit.

findings.suggestion: Keep kāja for leg, but replace the foot/pēda distractor (vocab-0135) in this question or supply a context that excludes the foot sense.
findings.reason: Actual LV→EN row presents leg as correct and foot as wrong for the bare prompt kāja. MLVV kāja sense 1.4 explicitly equals pēda, with everyday size/width examples. Thus foot is defensible without context. Actual EN→LV row likewise offers both kāja and pēda for leg, although that direction more naturally favors kāja; the decisive defect is LV→EN.

findings.suggestion: Keep vēders for belly/abdomen and everyday stomach; make the body-area sense explicit.
findings.reason: MLVV defines the abdominal body region and gives Sāp vēders. Russian живот and Japanese お腹 match it. The English word stomach must be understood colloquially here rather than as the specific digestive organ (kuņģis). No need to add the organ synonym to the active bank.

findings.suggestion: Keep paprika; clarify sweet/bell pepper in the shared meaning and English gloss.
findings.reason: MLVV paprika names the Capsicum plant and its fruit, with examples saldā paprika and stuffed paprika. Russian сладкий перец already specifies the vegetable. Broad English pepper can also mean the seasoning, for which paprika is not the intended general translation.

findings.suggestion: Keep malacis as conversational praise directed to a person, especially a child or familiar person; add that context to reference guidance.
findings.reason: MLVV labels malacis conversational and defines a person deserving praise. It is a natural child-facing equivalent of well done, not a defective literal translation. Do not imply a neutral evaluation of an object, workmanship, or formal praise to any stranger. The social-use recommendation remains editorial.

findings.suggestion: Keep ota; clarify paintbrush/brush for painting in the shared meaning and English gloss.
findings.reason: MLVV defines ota as a tool for painting. The school-art block supports this sense, but English brush alone also suggests hairbrushes or cleaning brushes. Context guidance preserves the valid LV word without introducing an unnecessary synonym.

findings.suggestion: Keep burts; clarify letter of the alphabet/written character.
findings.reason: MLVV defines a written symbol for a language sound. Russian буква and the language-learning block match that sense. English letter also means a written message, which is vēstule, so the shared sense should be explicit.

findings.suggestion: Keep vērot with watch/observe attentively as the intended sense; distinguish it from a generic watch-TV default and from skatīties uz (vocab-0432).
findings.reason: MLVV defines longer purposeful looking to find something out, with watching birds, surroundings and a live discussion as examples. This supports vērot rather than branding it unnatural. The broad English watch label hides that focused-observation sense; use a clear contextual gloss. Vocab-0432 actually offers vērot as a distractor for to look at: those verbs are related, but this review does not establish a second equally exact answer for that row.

findings.suggestion: Keep tev as to/for you addressed to one familiar person; explain that polite/plural addressing uses jums.
findings.reason: The existing dative is a natural short expression and reuses tu. It is not the neutral stranger-facing form for every English for you situation. MLVV supplies tev as the dative of familiar singular tu; no replacement is required for the intended casual context.

findings.suggestion: Keep tu for you (one familiar person); record jūs as the polite/plural distinction in reference guidance.
findings.reason: MLVV defines tu for relatives, friends and younger people. Russian ты agrees, but unqualified English you does not show number or politeness. The existing form belongs in a child/family course; it should not be presented as the default address to an unfamiliar adult.

notes: All 510 canonical meanings and LV forms were individually inspected from dist/audit-input.json, along with all 1530 actual LV distractor forms and their meaning labels. Cross-language LV/RU/EN bindings were consulted for sense and reverse-direction risks. Japanese is target-only and is not a Latvian-source or Latvian-target direction.
Every unflagged entry is a working keep, not native-speaker certification. This is a model/editorial audit with targeted dictionary corroboration; fluent Latvian human review is pending.

Findings are research proposals only. No active vocabulary, permanent concept meaning/binding, audio, application code or generated course asset was changed. Any later correction needs separate review and authorization.

The cited MLVV pages were retrieved for their definitions/examples. They support senses/register where stated, not corpus frequency or claims of a universal most-common wording. Recommendations about teaching defaults remain editorial.

Working keeps include sveiki as a normal hello, uz redzēšanos, lūdzu, palīdziet lūdzu, all man vajag practical requests, and the polite emergency calls. No stylistic reordering or extra grammatical complexity is proposed.
Working keeps include neutral māte/tēvs and affectionate vecmāmiņa/vectētiņš; family-affection wording is valid in child/family contexts and need not be replaced merely by another available synonym.

Common polysemy alone was not treated as an actual ambiguous question: roka arm/hand, kakls neck/throat, stunda hour/lesson, vārds word/name and grammatical gender forms were considered against the actual offered choices. Unoffered synonyms are not distractor defects.

No general hypernym/subtype overlap (for example meat versus chicken meat) was automatically counted as an equally exact translation; such choices still warrant fluent human validation. Only demonstrated competing translations were labeled ambiguous.

MLVV atlikums https://mlvv.tezaurs.lv/atlikums:1 explicitly includes Kasiere izdod atlikumu, supporting the existing cash-change translation. MLVV plauksta https://mlvv.tezaurs.lv/plauksta:1 explicitly includes delna/palm sense, supporting the existing palm translation. These were checked and kept.
All sources are actual retrieved URLs. An empty sources array means model-editorial/source-needed. No usage ranking, native certification, or exhaustive corpus search is claimed.
